Authors: Vijay V. Vazirani

The classic paper of Shapley and Shubik \cite{Shapley1971assignment} characterized the core of the assignment game. We observe that a sub-coalition consisting of one player (or a set of players from the same side of the bipartition) can make zero profit, and therefore its profit under a core imputation can be an arbitrary amount. Hence an arbitrary core imputation makes {\em no fairness guarantee at the level of individual agents}. Can this deficiency be addressed by picking a ``good'' core imputation? To arrive at an appropriate solution concept, we give specific criteria for picking a special core imputation, and we undertake a detailed comparison of four solution concepts. Leximin and leximax core imputations come out as clear winners; we define these to be {\em equitable core imputations}. These imputations achieve ``fairness'' in different ways: whereas leximin tries to make poor agents more rich, leximax tries to make rich agents less rich. We give combinatorial strongly polynomial algorithms for computing these imputations via a novel adaptation of the classical primal-dual paradigm. The ``engine'' driving them involves insights into core imputations obtained via complementarity. It will not be surprising if our work leads to new uses of this powerful technique. Furthermore, we expect more work on computing the leximin and leximax core imputations of other natural games, in addition to the recent follow-up work \cite{Leximin-max}.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We have considered multi-sided markets where agents are on an m-partite graph that induces a cycle-free network among the sectors. Basic coalitions do not need to have agents from all sectors, it is enough not to have two agents from the same sector. Moreover, the worth of a basic coalition is the addition of the worths of all its pairs that are an edge of the m-partite graph.

# Fair Core Imputations for the Assignment Game: New Solution Concepts and Efficient Algorithms

## Author

Listed:

  * Vijay V. Vazirani

Registered:

## Abstract

The assignment game is a classical model for profit sharing and a cornerstone of cooperative game theory. While an imputation in its core guarantees fairness among coalitions, it provides no fairness guarantee at the level of individual agents: single agents or one sided coalitions have zero standalone value and may receive arbitrarily small payoffs. Motivated by the growing focus on individual level fairness, we ask: Can one select a core imputation that is also fair to individuals? We introduce three individual fairness driven solution concepts, each promoting equity in a different way. The leximin and leximax core imputations extend max min and min max fairness to uplift the least advantaged and constrain the most advantaged agents, respectively. The min spread core imputation minimizes the gap between the largest and smallest positive payoffs, promoting equitable profit distribution. For all three solution concepts, we develop combinatorial, strongly polynomial algorithms. The leximin and leximax algorithms are based on a novel adaptation of the primal dual paradigm, while the min spread algorithm combines partial executions of the first two. We expect our work to revive innovation on the potent primal dual paradigm as well as promote further work on the algorithmic study of fairness and stability.

# Multi-sided assignment games on m-partite graphs

## Autors

Atay, Ata

Núñez, Marina (Núñez Oliva)

#### Resum

We consider a multi-sided assignment game with the following characteristics: (a) the agents are organized in m sectors that are connected by a graph that induces a weighted m-partite graph on the set of agents, (b) a basic coalition is formed by agents from different connected sectors, and (c) the worth of a basic coalition is the addition of the weights of all its pairs that belong to connected sectors. We provide a sufficient condition on the weights to guarantee balancedness of the related multi-sided assignment game. Moreover, when the graph on the sectors is cycle-free, we prove the game is strongly balanced and the core is fully described by means of the cores of the underlying two-sided assignment games associated with the edges of this graph. As a consequence, the complexity of the computation of an optimal matching is reduced and existence of optimal core allocations for each sector of the market is guaranteed.

L44: # Fair Core Imputations for the Assignment Game:
L45: New Solution Concepts and Efficient Algorithms
L46: 
L47: Vijay V. Vazirani Note: Supported in part by NSF grant CCF-2230414. Affiliation: University of California, Irvine
L48: ###### Abstract
L49: 
L50: The assignment game is a classical model for profit-sharing and a cornerstone of cooperative game theory. While an imputation in its core guarantees fairness among coalitions, it provides no fairness guarantee at the level of individual agents: single agents or one-sided coalitions have zero standalone value and may receive arbitrarily small payoffs. Motivated by the growing focus on individual-level fairness, we ask: Can one select a core imputation that is also fair to individuals?
L51: We introduce three individual-fairness-driven solution concepts, each promoting equity in a different way. The leximin and leximax core imputations extend max–min and min–max fairness to uplift the least advantaged and constrain the most advantaged agents, respectively. The min-spread core imputation minimizes the gap between the largest and smallest positive payoffs, promoting equitable profit distribution.
L52: For all three solution concepts, we develop combinatorial, strongly polynomial algorithms. The leximin and leximax algorithms are based on a novel adaptation of the primal–dual paradigm, while the min-spread algorithm combines partial executions of the first two. We expect our work to revive innovation on the potent primal-dual paradigm as well as promote further work on the algorithmic study of fairness and stability.
L53: ## 1 Introduction
L54: Fairness and equitable division have long been central themes in economics, from early social choice theory [cite32†2 ] to modern challenges in Internet resource allocation [cite33†37 ]. The study of fairness has come to a basic truth: no single definition can universally capture fairness, e.g., [cite34†40 ] lists 21 definitions! Within this vast literature, we are concerned with fairness at the level of coalitions and individual fairness.
L55: For the former, the core is the gold standard solution concept: it ensures that no coalition has an incentive to secede by guaranteeing each coalition at least as much profit as they can achieve on their own. Hence a core imputation guarantees stability by allocating a fair profit to each of exponentially many coalitions—a stringent requirement indeed.
L56: Recent work across game theory, networking and resource allocation has renewed attention on individual-level fairness as a fundamental consideration, e.g., the wide spread use of max-min and min-max fairness [cite35†41 , cite36†7 , cite37†39 , cite38†43 ], as well as their extensions to leximin and leximax allocations in modern applications such as fair rent division [cite39†18 ] and citizens’ assemblies [cite40†15 ].
L57: Our work bridges these two traditions in the context of the assignment game, which occupies a central place within cooperative game theory; the classic work of Shapley and Shubik [cite41†47 ] gave a complete characterization of its core, see Section cite10†3.1 . In this game, a coalition consisting of a single agent or a group from one side of the bipartition has zero standalone value.
L58: Consequently, under an arbitrary core imputation, individual agents are allowed to receive arbitrary profit shares, leading to inequity. To address this deficiency, we seek a core imputation that satisfies two key criteria:
L59:   1. 1.
L60: 
L61: The allocation of profit shares is individually fair.
L62: 
L63:   2. 2.
L64: 
L65: It is computable in polynomial—or preferably, strongly polynomial—time via a combinatorial algorithm^{1}^{1} 1 That is, the algorithm does not invoke an LP-solver, e.g., see [cite42†46 , cite43†33 ].
L66: We propose three solution concepts. All three deal with profit shares of essential agents, i.e., agents which are matched in every maximum weight matching, see Section cite11†4 ; these are the only agents which get positive profits in core imputations.
L67: 
L68:   1. 1.
L69: 
L70: the leximin core imputation, which extends max-min fairness by maximizing the smallest individual share and, subject to that, the next smallest, and so on;
L71: 
L72:   2. 2.
L73: the leximax core imputation, which symmetrically extends min-max fairness by minimizing the largest share, then the second largest, and so on;
L74: 
L75:   3. 3.
L76: 
L77: the min-spread core imputation, which minimizes the difference between the largest and smallest profit shares of essential agents.
L78: It is easy to see that none of these solution concepts dominates the others, e.g., see the example given in Section cite15†5 . Our solution concepts seek to reconcile the tension between coalitions demanding profit which is commensurate with their inherent worth and the societal norm of “equality” as a desirable outcome.
L79: Each promotes individual fairness in a distinct way: leximin uplifts the least advantaged, leximax reins in the most advantaged and min-spread makes individual profit shares as equal as possible. In Section cite15†5 we show that whereas leximin and leximax core imputations are unique, min-spread is not. In Section cite16†5.1 we show that the prominent solution concept of nucleolus does not promote individual fairness in any of these three ways, even for an infinite family of games, Theorem cite44†6 .
L80: We design combinatorial, strongly polynomial algorithms, having a running time of $O(mn^{3})$, for all three proposed solution concepts. For the leximin and leximax core imputations, our algorithms are based on a novel adaptation of the classical primal-dual paradigm; see Section cite7†1.1 . The algorithm for the min-spread solution is arguably even more innovative.
L81: It is made possible by the combinatorial nature of the previous two algorithms and is obtained by carefully orchestrating their partial executions, see Section cite27†10 .
L82: The assignment and stable matching games share a key structural property: in both, the set of solutions forms a distributive lattice, with the top and bottom elements favoring opposite sides of the bipartition (see details in Section cite8†2 ). These extreme solutions are efficiently computable in both settings. However, while the stable matching lattice is finite—enabling the design of algorithms for finding more equitable outcomes—the lattice of core imputations in the assignment game is infinite.
L83: This fundamental difference precludes the use of Birkhoff’s Representation Theorem and necessitates a fundamentally new approach to identifying individually fair core imputations.
L84: We anticipate that the novel way of running the primal-dual method proposed here will not only be exploited for additional applications, but it will also revive innovation on this highly potent method^{2}^{2} 2 This is the reason we preferred submitting this paper to a theory, rather than an AGT, conference.. Additionally, we expect our work to promote further work on the algorithmic study of fairness and stability, as was done in [cite45†20 ].
L85: ### 1.1 How was the Primal-Dual Framework Adapted to our Problem?
L86: 
L87: The primal-dual method has three distinguishing features:
L88: 
L89:   1. 1.
L90: 
L91: It provides a flexible, high level framework whose details can be tailored to the specific problem at hand.
L92: 
L93:   2. 2.
L94: 
L95: It achieves global optimality or near-optimality through a sequence of local improvements.
L96: 
L97:   3. 3.
L98: 
L99: It leads to efficient, combinatorial algorithms.
L100: The method achieved major successes, first in combinatorial optimization [cite43†33 , cite42†46 ] and then in approximation algorithms [cite46†51 ]. These settings involved finding an integral optimal (or near-optimal) solution to the primal LP, together with an optimal (or near-optimal) solution to the dual LP. Complementary slackness conditions — or an appropriate relaxation of these conditions — helped transform the global task into a sequence of local tasks.
L101: Following these successes, researchers adapted it to solve rational convex programs, i.e., non-linear convex programs that always admit rational solutions, defined in [cite47†52 ]. These include [cite48†10 , cite49†28 , cite47†52 , cite50†11 ]. Indeed, today it is appropriate to call this method the primal-dual paradigm.
L102: Despite its versatility, it was not initially clear that this method would be suitable for our setting. In our case, computing an optimal solution to the primal and dual LPs — namely, a maximum-weight matching and an associated core imputation — is straightforward. However, the core challenge lies in transforming this arbitrary core imputation into the leximin or leximax core imputation.
L103: One might consider locally improving the imputation while maintaining the optimality of both primal and dual solutions. However, because the primal-dual pair satisfies all complementary slackness conditions, how will the global problem be broken into local steps? To address this, we introduce a novel coordinating mechanism: a clock that governs the algorithm’s progress and synchronizes all updates.
L104: For each time $t$, we can define a vertex set $W_{t}\subseteq(U\cup V)$ such that in the induced subgraph $H_{t}$ of $G$, the profit shares form the unique leximin core imputation for $H_{t}$^{3}^{3} 3 The proof of this fact crucially depends on the correct resolution of some subtle algorithmic choices, see Sections cite21†7.2 and cite23†7.4 .. We prove that in polynomial time $W_{t}=(U\cup V)$, hence terminating in the required imputation.
L105: The proof of this fact crucially depends on the correct resolution of some subtle algorithmic choices, see Sections cite21†7.2 and cite23†7.4 .
L106: While prior primal-dual algorithms have employed the notion of time, our use of it is distinct in both purpose and prominence. For example, in [cite51†27 ], dual variables evolve over time, but this evolution is used merely to enforce relaxed complementary slackness conditions, which remain the primary engine for local-to-global transformation. Similarly, in [cite49†28 ], time progression aids in ensuring cross-monotonicity in cost-sharing methods, rather than in structuring the optimization process itself.
L107: In contrast, in our approach, time is the central coordinating device that transforms the global optimization problem into a sequence of structured local updates.
L108: The broad outline given above is far from sufficient for designing the entire algorithm. The latter requires a precise understanding of the way core imputations allocate the total profit to agents and teams; in particular, we need to answer the following questions:
L109:

L123: Comparison with the stable matching game: A useful perspective is provided by the stable matching game of Gale and Shapley [cite52†19 ], which is a non-transferable utility (NTU) game. The core of this game is the set of all stable matchings — each ensures that no coalition formed by one agent from each side of the bipartition has an incentive to secede. It is well known that this set forms a finite distributive lattice.
L124: Its top and bottom elements maximally favor one side and disfavor the other side of the bipartition, and the Deferred Acceptance Algorithm [cite52†19 ] computes precisely these two extremes.
L125: However, in many applications, one desires stable matchings that are more equitable to both sides. L88: ## 2 The multi-sided assignment problem on an m-partite graph and its related coalitional game
L89: Let N be the finite set of agents in a market situation. The set N is partitioned in m sets \(N_1, N_2, \ldots , N_m\), each sector maybe representing a set of agents with a specific role in the market.
L90: There is a graph \(\overline{G}\) with set of nodes \(\{N_1,N_2,\ldots ,N_m\}\), that we simply denote \(\{1,2,\ldots ,m\}\) when no confusion arises, and we will identify the graph with its set of edges.^{cite43†Footnote 1 } The graph \(\overline{G}\) induces another graph G on the set of agents N such that \(\{i,j\}\in G\) if and only if there exist \(r,s\in \{1,2,\ldots ,m\}\) such that \(r\ne s\), \(i\in N_r\), \(j\in N_s\) and \(\{r,s\}\in \overline{G}\).
L91: Notice that the graph G is an m-partite graph, that meaning that two agents on the same sector are not connected in G. We say that graph \(\overline{G}\) is the quotient graph of G.^{cite44†Footnote 2 }
L92: For any pair of connected sectors \(\{r,s\}\in \overline{G}\), there is a non-negative valuation matrix \(A^{\{r,s\}}\) and for all \(i\in N_r\) and \(j\in N_s\), \(v(\{i,j\})=a_{ij}^{\{r,s\}}\) represents the value obtained by the cooperation of agents i and j.
L93: Notice that these valuation matrices, \(A=\{A^{\{r,s\}}\}_{\{r,s\}\in \overline{G}}\), determine a system of weights on the graph G, and for each pair of connected sectors \(\{r,s\}\in \overline{G}\), \((N_r, N_s, A^{\{r,s\}})\) defines a bilateral assignment market. Sometimes, to simplify notation, we will write \(A^{rs}\), with \(r<s\), instead of \(A^{\{r,s\}}\).
L94: Then, \(\gamma =(N_1,N_2,\ldots ,N_m; G; \{A^{\{r,s\}}\}_{\{r,s\}\in \overline{G}})\) is a multi-sided assignment market on an m-partite graph. When necessary, we will write \(G^A\) to denote the weighted graph with the nodes and edges of G and the weights defined by the matrices \(\{A^{\{r,s\}}\}_{\{r,s\}\in \overline{G}}\).
L95: Given any such market \(\gamma \), a coalition \(S\subseteq N\) defines a submarket \(\gamma _{|S}=(S\cap N_1,\ldots , S\cap N_m; G_{|S}; A_{|S})\) where \(G_{|S}\) is the subgraph of G defined by the nodes in S and \(A_{|S}\) consists of the values of A that correspond to edges \(\{i,j\}\) in the subgraph \(G_{|S}\).
L96: We now introduce a coalitional game related to the above market situation. To this end, we first define the worth of some coalitions that we name basic coalitions and then the worth of arbitrary coalitions will be obtained by just imposing superadditivity. A basic coalition E is a subset of agents belonging to sectors that are connected in the quotient graph \(\overline{G}\) and with no two agents of the same sector.

L127: A multi-sided assignment game on an m-partite graph is balanced if it has a non-empty core. Moreover, and following Le Breton et al. L128: Our aim is to study whether this property extends to m-partite graphs or whether balancedness depends on properties of the weights or the structure of the graph.

L39:   * cite21†Explore all metrics L40: ## Abstract
L41: We consider a three-sided market where each buyer-seller pair can attain a profit only if there is a middleman that connects them. This profit does not depend on the identity of the middlemen, and each buyer and seller can take part in at most one partnership while middlemen can establish multiple partnerships, up to their capacity.
L42: We show that the core is non-empty and strictly contains the set of competitive equilibrium payoff vectors that coincides with the set of solutions of the dual q-assignment problem, where q is the total capacity of the middlemen.
L43: ## 1 Introduction
L44: In a two-sided market there are two disjoint finite sets of buyers and sellers that want to trade indivisible units of some good. Each buyer wants to buy one unit and each seller has only one unit on sale. Each buyer may place different values on the units of different sellers and a valuation matrix gathers the values of trade between all possible buyer-seller pairs. This is the setting of the assignment game introduced by Shapley and Shubik (cite22†1972 ).
L45: The worth of a coalition of agents is the maximum value that can be obtained by matching buyers and sellers in the coalition. Utility is fully transferable by means of the price a buyer pays for the assigned object and then the core consists of the set of payoff vectors (one payoff to each agent) such that no coalition blocks since it obtains at least its worth. Shapley and Shubik prove that the core of the assignment game is non-empty and each core allocation is supported by competitive prices.
L46: The core not only coincides with the set of competitive equilibrium payoff vectors but also with the set of solutions of the dual assignment problem, that is, the dual problem to the linear program that finds an optimal matching for the grand coalition.
L47: In the present paper we assume buyers and sellers cannot meet directly. A middleman is needed to connect a buyer with a seller, and this middleman may connect several buyer-seller pairs, up to a given capacity. We assume then there is a third side in the market formed by a finite set of middlemen (disjoint with the set of buyers and sellers).
L48: This situation may represent a real estate market in which value is generated by the matching of a buyer and a seller but typically real estate agencies act as intermediaries. A house can be advertised in the website of several agencies, and each buyer also searches in several of these sites. Moreover which middleman participates in the sale of a house does not affect how much the buyers value this house.
L49: This situation resembles the firm-supplier–buyer situation in Stuart (cite23†1997 ), but there the value of a triplet is the sum of the value generated by the firm and the supplier and the value generated by supplier and buyer. In our case the middleman does not modify the value of the buyer-seller pair, that is, the profit generated by the trade of a buyer and a seller does not depend on who is the intermediary that connects them. Stuart’s model is a particular instance of three-sided assignment game.
L50: Because the value of a firm-supplier–buyer triplet is defined additively, it can be guaranteed that the core of the associated three-sided assignment game is non-empty. It is also known, see Kaneko and Wooders (cite24†1982 ), that three-sided assignment games where values of triplets are defined arbitrarily may have an empty core.
L51: Different to our model, each supplier in Stuart’s model has unitary capacity, that is, each supplier can only connect one firm-buyer pair. Hence, the assignment markets with middlemen we consider here are three-sided assignment markets with multiple partnership (on the side of middlemen). Two-sided assignment markets with multiple partnership have been studied for instance in Kaneko (cite25†1976 ), Thompson (cite26†1980 ), Sotomayor (cite27†1992 ), Sotomayor (cite28†2002 ) and Sánchez-Soriano et al. (cite29†2001 ).
L52: When both sides of the market allow for multiple-partnership and each buyer-seller pair can trade more than one unit, these games are sometimes called transportation games.
L53: Transportation games have a non-empty core and this core contains the set of competitive equilibrium payoff vectors but, different to the one-to-one assignment game, this inclusion may be strict, that is, not all core allocations are supported by competitive prices. Also, the set of competitive payoff vectors (strictly) includes the set of solutions of the dual assignment problem.
L54: It is shown in Sotomayor (cite28†2002 ) that most of the properties of the core of the one-to-one assignment game, such as the lattice structure and the opposition of interest between the two sides of the market, are lost when we allow for multiple partnership.
L55: After defining the model of assignment games with middlemen in Sect. cite30†2 , in Sect. cite31†3 we show that assignment games with middlemen, where the profit of a buyer-seller pair does not depend on who is the middleman that connects them, always have a non-empty core. When the number of middlemen in the market is enough to connect the maximum possible number of buyer-seller pairs, core elements can be obtained from the dual two-sided assignment problem.
L56: Otherwise, when the total capacity of middlemen is scarce, we will use a result on the totally-unimodularity of the matrix of coefficients of the q-cardinality assignment problem (Dell’amico and Martello cite32†1997 ).
L57: Obviously, if we were to assume that the profit of a buyer-seller pair does depend on who is the middleman that connects them, then assignment games with middlemen would be arbitrary three-sided assignment games as in Kaneko and Wooders (cite24†1982 ) and hence the core might be empty.
L58: Once we know the core of the assignment game with middlemen is non-empty, we analyze if all core allocations are supported by competitive prices. The answer is negative, but we characterize the set of competitive equilibrium payoffs as the set of solutions of the dual assignment problem. In this way, we generalize to this three-sided case the results obtained by Kaneko (cite25†1976 ) for two-sided markets where sellers can establish multiple partnership.
L59: The study of the role of middlemen in more general markets is well known in the literature. Kalai et al. (cite33†1978 ) study exchange economies with three agents and compares the core of the game under free trade or imposing that any trade must be done by means of a middlemen. Rubinstein and Wolinsky (cite34†1987 ) study markets with three sectors, where buyers and sellers may trade directly or by means of a middlemen. These intermediaries buy units of homogeneous goods from producers and sell to consumers.
L60: The problem is dynamic and the presence of middlemen shortens the period a buyer-seller pair has to wait for a transaction and hence decreases the searching costs. In this same searching framework, Shevchenko (cite35†2004 ) considers a variety of goods and analyzes the role of middlemen that hold inventories of many goods and Johri and Leach (cite36†2002 ) study a general equilibrium model where some agents choose whether to become producers or middlemen.
L61: A different approach can be found in Blume et al. (cite37†2009 ) where agents in a three-sided market are connected by means of a network, that indicates with which middlemen each buyer and seller can trade. The authors study a strategic game where first each middleman sets a bid price and an ask price to each seller and buyer to whom he is connected, and secondly each buyer and each seller accepts only one offer.
L62: Subgame perfect equilibria of this trading networks where middlemen set prices always exist and lead to an efficient allocation of the goods.
L63: Our approach is not dynamic and it is more on the line of Kalai et al. (cite33†1978 ) but assuming agents are partitioned in different sectors. We are even more related to Oishi and Sakaue (cite38†2014 ) and Atay et al. (cite39†2023 ) who also introduce middlemen in the assignment game but allow buyers and sellers to trade either with or without middlemen.
L64: In the first of the aforementioned references, each middleman has unitary capacity, while in the second each middlemen has unconstrained capacity and the value of a buyer-seller trade depends on the middleman that participates. In both cases the non-emptiness of the core is guaranteed by allowing buyers and sellers to trade directly if necessary.
L363: Notice that \(p\le 8\), to guarantee \(u_3+w_2=8-p\ge 0\). And indeed the payoff vector (0, 2, 0; 8, 8; 0, 0, 4) is competitive. Morevover, \((4-p)+(7-p)\le u_3 + w_2=8-p\) implies \(p\ge 3\), and the reader can check that (0, 4, 1; 3, 3; 0, 4, 7) is a competitive payoff vector since it satisfies all the above constraints. In this example, the interval of competitive prices for the middlemen is \([\underline{p}, \overline{p}]=[3, 8]\).
L364: ## 5 Concluding remarks
L365: This papers shows a class of three-sided assignment games for which the core is non-empty. The condition that defines this class is not in terms of some additivity of the valuations, as it is the case for other classes of three-sided assignment games with non-empty cores (Quint cite54†1991 ; Stuart cite23†1997 ; Tejada cite55†2013 ), but the fact that one side of the market, the middlemen, does not affect the valuations of pairs from the other sides (buyer-seller pairs).
L366: We think this assumption is quite realistic when considering middlemen, taking for instance real estate markets.
L367: Oishi and Sakaue (cite38†2014 ) also consider competitive equilibria in assignment markets with middlemen, but, to the best of our knowledge, in their paper middlemen only have capacity one and it is assumed that there are always enough middlemen to connect the maximum possible number of buyer-seller pairs. In Atay et al.
L368: (cite39†2023 ), the notion of competitive prices is not the standard in assignment games with multiple partnership (see Sotomayor (cite56†2007 )) since they assume a middleman may receive different prices for its service to different buyers.

L39:   * cite21†Explore all metrics L40: ## Abstract
L41: We consider a three-sided market where each buyer-seller pair can attain a profit only if there is a middleman that connects them. This profit does not depend on the identity of the middlemen, and each buyer and seller can take part in at most one partnership while middlemen can establish multiple partnerships, up to their capacity.
L42: We show that the core is non-empty and strictly contains the set of competitive equilibrium payoff vectors that coincides with the set of solutions of the dual q-assignment problem, where q is the total capacity of the middlemen.
L43: ## 1 Introduction
L44: In a two-sided market there are two disjoint finite sets of buyers and sellers that want to trade indivisible units of some good. Each buyer wants to buy one unit and each seller has only one unit on sale. Each buyer may place different values on the units of different sellers and a valuation matrix gathers the values of trade between all possible buyer-seller pairs. This is the setting of the assignment game introduced by Shapley and Shubik (cite22†1972 ).
L45: The worth of a coalition of agents is the maximum value that can be obtained by matching buyers and sellers in the coalition. Utility is fully transferable by means of the price a buyer pays for the assigned object and then the core consists of the set of payoff vectors (one payoff to each agent) such that no coalition blocks since it obtains at least its worth. Shapley and Shubik prove that the core of the assignment game is non-empty and each core allocation is supported by competitive prices.
L46: The core not only coincides with the set of competitive equilibrium payoff vectors but also with the set of solutions of the dual assignment problem, that is, the dual problem to the linear program that finds an optimal matching for the grand coalition.
L47: In the present paper we assume buyers and sellers cannot meet directly. A middleman is needed to connect a buyer with a seller, and this middleman may connect several buyer-seller pairs, up to a given capacity. We assume then there is a third side in the market formed by a finite set of middlemen (disjoint with the set of buyers and sellers).
L48: This situation may represent a real estate market in which value is generated by the matching of a buyer and a seller but typically real estate agencies act as intermediaries. A house can be advertised in the website of several agencies, and each buyer also searches in several of these sites. Moreover which middleman participates in the sale of a house does not affect how much the buyers value this house.
L49: This situation resembles the firm-supplier–buyer situation in Stuart (cite23†1997 ), but there the value of a triplet is the sum of the value generated by the firm and the supplier and the value generated by supplier and buyer. In our case the middleman does not modify the value of the buyer-seller pair, that is, the profit generated by the trade of a buyer and a seller does not depend on who is the intermediary that connects them. Stuart’s model is a particular instance of three-sided assignment game.
L50: Because the value of a firm-supplier–buyer triplet is defined additively, it can be guaranteed that the core of the associated three-sided assignment game is non-empty. It is also known, see Kaneko and Wooders (cite24†1982 ), that three-sided assignment games where values of triplets are defined arbitrarily may have an empty core.
L51: Different to our model, each supplier in Stuart’s model has unitary capacity, that is, each supplier can only connect one firm-buyer pair. Hence, the assignment markets with middlemen we consider here are three-sided assignment markets with multiple partnership (on the side of middlemen). Two-sided assignment markets with multiple partnership have been studied for instance in Kaneko (cite25†1976 ), Thompson (cite26†1980 ), Sotomayor (cite27†1992 ), Sotomayor (cite28†2002 ) and Sánchez-Soriano et al. (cite29†2001 ).
L52: When both sides of the market allow for multiple-partnership and each buyer-seller pair can trade more than one unit, these games are sometimes called transportation games.
L53: Transportation games have a non-empty core and this core contains the set of competitive equilibrium payoff vectors but, different to the one-to-one assignment game, this inclusion may be strict, that is, not all core allocations are supported by competitive prices. Also, the set of competitive payoff vectors (strictly) includes the set of solutions of the dual assignment problem.
L54: It is shown in Sotomayor (cite28†2002 ) that most of the properties of the core of the one-to-one assignment game, such as the lattice structure and the opposition of interest between the two sides of the market, are lost when we allow for multiple partnership.
L55: After defining the model of assignment games with middlemen in Sect. cite30†2 , in Sect. cite31†3 we show that assignment games with middlemen, where the profit of a buyer-seller pair does not depend on who is the middleman that connects them, always have a non-empty core. When the number of middlemen in the market is enough to connect the maximum possible number of buyer-seller pairs, core elements can be obtained from the dual two-sided assignment problem.
L56: Otherwise, when the total capacity of middlemen is scarce, we will use a result on the totally-unimodularity of the matrix of coefficients of the q-cardinality assignment problem (Dell’amico and Martello cite32†1997 ).
L57: Obviously, if we were to assume that the profit of a buyer-seller pair does depend on who is the middleman that connects them, then assignment games with middlemen would be arbitrary three-sided assignment games as in Kaneko and Wooders (cite24†1982 ) and hence the core might be empty.
L58: Once we know the core of the assignment game with middlemen is non-empty, we analyze if all core allocations are supported by competitive prices. The answer is negative, but we characterize the set of competitive equilibrium payoffs as the set of solutions of the dual assignment problem. In this way, we generalize to this three-sided case the results obtained by Kaneko (cite25†1976 ) for two-sided markets where sellers can establish multiple partnership.
L59: The study of the role of middlemen in more general markets is well known in the literature. Kalai et al. (cite33†1978 ) study exchange economies with three agents and compares the core of the game under free trade or imposing that any trade must be done by means of a middlemen. Rubinstein and Wolinsky (cite34†1987 ) study markets with three sectors, where buyers and sellers may trade directly or by means of a middlemen. These intermediaries buy units of homogeneous goods from producers and sell to consumers.
L60: The problem is dynamic and the presence of middlemen shortens the period a buyer-seller pair has to wait for a transaction and hence decreases the searching costs. In this same searching framework, Shevchenko (cite35†2004 ) considers a variety of goods and analyzes the role of middlemen that hold inventories of many goods and Johri and Leach (cite36†2002 ) study a general equilibrium model where some agents choose whether to become producers or middlemen.
L61: A different approach can be found in Blume et al. (cite37†2009 ) where agents in a three-sided market are connected by means of a network, that indicates with which middlemen each buyer and seller can trade. The authors study a strategic game where first each middleman sets a bid price and an ask price to each seller and buyer to whom he is connected, and secondly each buyer and each seller accepts only one offer.
L62: Subgame perfect equilibria of this trading networks where middlemen set prices always exist and lead to an efficient allocation of the goods.
L63: Our approach is not dynamic and it is more on the line of Kalai et al. (cite33†1978 ) but assuming agents are partitioned in different sectors. We are even more related to Oishi and Sakaue (cite38†2014 ) and Atay et al. (cite39†2023 ) who also introduce middlemen in the assignment game but allow buyers and sellers to trade either with or without middlemen.
L64: In the first of the aforementioned references, each middleman has unitary capacity, while in the second each middlemen has unconstrained capacity and the value of a buyer-seller trade depends on the middleman that participates. In both cases the non-emptiness of the core is guaranteed by allowing buyers and sellers to trade directly if necessary.
L65: The main objective of the present paper is to show that even when we impose that all trades are done by means of a middlemen and allow that the capacity of the set of middlemen may not be enough to support all profitable buyer-seller trades, the core is still non-empty. The middlemen do not buy the goods, simply connect buyers and sellers and get a payoff when the trade is done.
L66: We also assume any middleman in the market can support any buyer-seller trade, this is not unusual nowadays when you can find the same houses announced in most of the important websites that operate in a given area. But since the operating capacity of the intermediary firm may differ, buyers often have to approach more than one firm to reach the desired house. Also, when analyzing competitive equilibria, and because middlemen do not buy any object but offer a service, differently from Blume et al.
L67: (cite37†2009 ), both middlemen and sellers set prices.
L68: After the analysis of the core in Sect. cite31†3 , in Sect. cite40†4 we define competitive prices and competitive equilibrium payoff vectors and study the relationship between this set and the core and also with the set of solutions of the dual assignment problem. Section cite41†5 concludes.
